% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{abstract}
We present a battery of \TotalRuns{} three-dimensional N-body simulations
testing which initial summaries of particle structure and phase-space
information carry predictive power for future gravitational clustering.
The battery spans $N \in [\NParticleMin{}, \NParticleMax{}]$ particles,
softening lengths $\heps \in [\EpsMin{}, \EpsMax{}]$, \NICs{} initial
condition families, and \NModels{} force-model classes, with \NReplicates{}
independent realisations per parameter cell.
The result is not a universal ranking: which description best predicts
later clustering depends on both the initial condition family and the
observable class.
Bimodal (two-cluster) initial conditions define a robust coarse-dominance
regime in which the initial large-scale density variance predicts future
clustering with $r = \BimodalCoarseR{}$ (95\% CI
$[\BimodalCoarseCILo{}, \BimodalCoarseCIHi{}]$) at representative
$N = 1024$, $\heps = 0.05$; this bimodal verdict holds without exception across the
full parameter sweep.
None of the tested positional fine observables---local kNN density, small-scale
Fourier power, close-pair fraction---outperforms the coarse predictor for
this family.
Concentrated profiles (Hernquist, Plummer) show a suggestive fine-leaning VelDisp
signal at small softening; the 95\% confidence intervals include zero
at the current replicate count and the pattern is not robustly established.
Tested positional fine observables do not outperform the coarse predictor
for concentrated profiles either.
The boundary between regimes appears to be governed in part by the
softening-to-scale-radius ratio: the VelDisp signal weakens substantially
by $\heps = \EpsMax{}$.
These results show that in 3D self-gravitating N-body systems,
predictive advantage is family-dependent and observable-class-dependent:
bimodal mergers robustly favor coarse density structure, whereas
concentrated profiles show only a suggestive fine-kinematic signal at
small softening, with no tested positional fine observable outperforming
the coarse predictor.
\end{abstract}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The evolution of a self-gravitating system depends on how mass is distributed
at initialisation and on how that distribution links to the future trajectory
of the phase-space density.
A practical question in computational dynamics is which initial summary
statistic best predicts future clustering---a question that becomes sharp
when available observables belong to qualitatively different classes:
large-scale density contrast (coarse), local positional structure
(fine positional), and phase-space substructure (fine kinematic).

The Jeans instability criterion provides a physical prior.
Instability occurs at wavelengths comparable to the Jeans length
$\lambda_J \propto \sigma_v \rho^{-1/2}$, suggesting that large-scale
density contrast---the coarse description---should dominate future clustering
\citep{BinneyTremaine2008}.
This motivates a systematic test: does the Jeans prior hold empirically
across N-body initial condition families, and if so, under what
observable-class and softening conditions?

We study four initial condition families spanning qualitatively distinct
structural types (Section~\ref{sec:ics}): a two-cluster merger (bimodal),
a Hernquist cusp \citep{Hernquist1990}, a Plummer sphere \citep{Plummer1911},
and a cold multi-clump configuration.
For each we test observables belonging to three classes---coarse positional,
fine positional, and fine kinematic---using Pearson correlation with bootstrap
confidence intervals as the verdict criterion.

The paper is organised as follows.
Section~\ref{sec:methods} describes force models, integrators, and battery
design.
Section~\ref{sec:ics} introduces the initial condition families.
Section~\ref{sec:observables} defines the observable classes and statistical
protocol.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents the results in order from hard anchor to
boundary map.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} interprets the findings and states explicitly
what is and is not earned.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} states the conclusions.


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Models and Numerical Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Force models}

Two force-model classes are compared as distinct physics.

\textit{Direct-sum isolated} (\texttt{direct\_isolated}).
Forces are computed via the softened pairwise potential
$\phi_{ij} = -Gm(r_{ij}^2 + \heps^2)^{-1/2}$
at $O(N^2)$ cost.
The domain is open; all observables use a discard-outside rule restricting
measurements to $[0,L)^3$, so coarse and fine observables share identical
particle sets.

\textit{Particle-mesh periodic} (\texttt{pm\_periodic}).
The density field is deposited via cloud-in-cell (CIC) interpolation onto
a $32^3$ grid; the Poisson equation is solved spectrally by fast Fourier
transform \citep{HockneyEastwood1988}.
Periodic boundary conditions are enforced.
The PM Hamiltonian differs from the direct-sum Hamiltonian; the two model
classes represent distinct physics and are compared in
Section~\ref{sec:results:model_compare}.

\subsection{Integrator}

Both models use leapfrog KDK (kick-drift-kick) with fixed time step
$\delta t = 0.005$, $G = 1$, unit total mass, and box size $L = 2$
\citep{Quinn1997,Yoshida1990}.
Total integration: \NSteps{} steps ($t_{\rm final} = 3.0$ in natural units).
Snapshots at steps 0, \HEarly{}, \HMid{}, and \NSteps{}.

\subsection{Battery design}

The battery spans $N \in \{256, 512, 1024, 2048\}$,
$\heps \in \{0.02, 0.05, 0.10\}$, two force models, four initial
condition families, and \NReplicates{} independent realisations per cell.
Each replicate uses a distinct random seed for particle placement drawn
from the IC distribution; all other parameters are held fixed.
Replicates therefore capture sampling variance in the initial structural
observables, which drives variance in future clustering outcomes and
makes the Pearson correlations estimable.
This yields \NCells{} parameter cells and \TotalRuns{} total runs.
Bootstrap CIs use \NBootstrap{} resamples per cell.

The bimodal IC gives each sub-cluster an infall velocity of
$0.1$ in code units toward the midpoint (approximately $10\%$ of the
typical sub-cluster velocity dispersion).
Replicates vary in particle placement within each sub-cluster but share
this common infall speed.

The ClosePairs observable is defined as pairs within $4\heps$.
Across the $\heps$ sweep this measures three different physical scales
($0.08$, $0.20$, $0.40$ in box units), which complicates direct
cross-$\heps$ comparison for this observable relative to the others.


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Initial Condition Families}
\label{sec:ics}

Figure~\ref{fig:ic_gallery} shows all four families as projected density
images for $N = \ShowcaseN{}$.
The families span large-scale topology and inner-profile shape.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig01_ic_gallery.pdf}
\caption{Initial condition families at $N = \ShowcaseN{}$, direct-isolated,
  $\heps = 0.05$.
  Each panel shows projected density on a $128^2$ grid (log scale).
  Left to right, top to bottom: bimodal (two-cluster), Hernquist,
  Plummer, cold-clumpy.}
\label{fig:ic_gallery}
\end{figure}

\textit{Bimodal} (\texttt{bimodal3d}).
Two equal-mass Plummer sub-clusters of scale radius $a = 0.10$ placed
at $\pm 0.25\,L$ along the $x$-axis with an infall velocity of $0.1$ code
units toward the midpoint (approximately $10\%$ of the sub-cluster velocity
dispersion).
Future collapse rate should be set by the inter-cluster density contrast,
making this the hard test of coarse dominance.

\textit{Hernquist} (\texttt{hernquist3d}).
Drawn from $\rho \propto r^{-1}(r+a)^{-3}$ \citep{Hernquist1990}
with $a = 0.20$, velocities from an isotropic Gaussian at
$\sigma \approx (G/6a)^{1/2}$.
The steep inner cusp concentrates kinematic energy at small radii.

\textit{Plummer} (\texttt{plummer3d}).
Drawn from $\rho \propto (r^2+a^2)^{-5/2}$ \citep{Plummer1911}
with $a = 0.20$.
Softer core than Hernquist; less concentrated velocity field.

\textit{Cold-clumpy} (\texttt{cold\_clumpy3d}).
Five equal-mass Plummer sub-clusters with random positions and cold
internal dispersions ($\sigma_{\rm inner} = 0.05$).


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Observables and Statistical Design}
\label{sec:observables}

\subsection{Observable classes}

\textbf{Coarse positional.}
Density variance on a regular $g^3$ grid,
$\sigrho(g) = \mathrm{Var}[\rho_{\mathbf{i}}]$,
for $g \in \{4, 8, 16\}$.
Primary coarse observable: $\sigrho(8)$ (CoarseG8).

\textbf{Fine positional} (three observables).
(i)~kNN-all: mean $k$-nearest-neighbour density over all in-box particles
at $k = 16$.
(ii)~Pk: power in Fourier modes with $|\mathbf{k}| > g/4$.
(iii)~ClosePairs: fraction of pairs within $4\heps$.

\textbf{Fine kinematic.}
Local velocity dispersion
$\sigma_v^{\rm loc}(i) = \langle\|\mathbf{v}_j -
\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathcal{N}(i)}\|^2\rangle^{1/2}_{j\in\mathcal{N}_k(i)}$
averaged over all in-box particles (VelDisp).
This is the only observable accessing phase-space information.

\textbf{Fine structural.}
FoF group count at linking length $b = 0.20\,\bar{d}$ (recorded; included
in the summary matrix).

\subsection{Prediction target and verdict criterion}

Primary target: $\dCearly$, the change in $\sigrho(8)$ between $t=0$ and
step \HEarly{}.
Verdict: \textsc{coarse} if $|r_{\rm best\,coarse}| - |r_{\rm best\,fine}| > 0.05$,
\textsc{fine} if reversed, tie otherwise (threshold set a priori).
Pearson correlations are computed across the \NReplicates{} replicates per cell.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Numerical credibility}
\label{sec:results:diag}

Table~\ref{tab:diagnostics} and Figure~\ref{fig:diagnostics} summarise
conservation diagnostics for all direct-isolated runs.
The median relative energy drift is $\EnergyDriftMedian{}$
(maximum $\EnergyDriftMax{}$).
All families show drift below $10^{-3}$, confirming that leapfrog KDK
is well-behaved across the full $N$--$\heps$ grid.
Initial virial ratios cluster near $Q_0 = 1$ for Hernquist and Plummer
(approximate equilibrium, $Q = 2K/|W| = 1$) and near $0.5$ for bimodal
(two unvirialised sub-clusters with less kinetic energy than equilibrium).
There is no obvious drift-outcome trend visible in the diagnostics.
PM periodic runs do not permit direct energy bookkeeping because their
Hamiltonian differs from the direct-sum Hamiltonian.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Conservation diagnostics (direct-isolated model).
  Median and maximum relative energy drift $\Delta E/E_0$ and mean final
  virial ratio $Q_f = 2K_f/|W_f|$, aggregated over all $N$ and $\heps$ within
  each IC family.
  The bimodal family reaches $Q_f \gg 1$, indicating that by
  $t_{\rm final} = 3.0$ the post-merger remnant remains dynamically hot
  and has not yet virialised.
  PM periodic entries are n/a.}
\label{tab:diagnostics}
\input{outputs/tables/diagnostics.tex}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig09_diagnostics.pdf}
\caption{\textit{Left}: distribution of $\log_{10}(\Delta E/E_0)$ by IC family
  (direct-isolated).
  \textit{Centre}: initial virial ratio $Q_0 = 2K/|W|$ by family; dashed
  line marks virial equilibrium $Q = 1$.
  \textit{Right}: energy drift vs final virial ratio.
  No drift-outcome correlation is present.}
\label{fig:diagnostics}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Hard anchor: bimodal coarse dominance}
\label{sec:results:bimodal}

The bimodal initial condition is the paper's hard anchor.
Figure~\ref{fig:bimodal_anchor} shows (left) the scatter of initial
$\sigrho(8)$ against $\dCearly$ across \NReplicates{} replicates at
$N = 1024$, $\heps = 0.05$, and (right) $|r|$ for CoarseG8 and the
best fine observable as a function of softening $\heps$.
The coarse predictor achieves $r = \BimodalCoarseR{}$
(CI $[\BimodalCoarseCILo{}, \BimodalCoarseCIHi{}]$).
The best fine observable in this cell achieves $r = \BimodalBestFineR{}$.
The gap is $\BimodalGap{}$ in absolute $r$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig04_bimodal_anchor.pdf}
\caption{Bimodal hard anchor: $N = 1024$, $\heps = 0.05$,
  direct-isolated, \NReplicates{} replicates.
  \textit{Left}: initial $\sigrho(8)$ vs $\dCearly$ with least-squares fit.
  \textit{Right}: $|r|$ for CoarseG8 (blue) and best fine observable (grey)
  vs softening $\heps$. Coarse dominates at all tested softening values.}
\label{fig:bimodal_anchor}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling} shows N-scaling from \BimodalNRange{} particles.
The coarse predictor is stable in the range
$r \in [\BimodalNScaleMin{}, \BimodalNScaleMax{}]$, and the verdict
is \textsc{coarse} in every cell across all $N$, all $\heps$, and both
force models.
None of the tested positional fine observables outperforms the coarse
predictor in any bimodal cell.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{N-scaling summary for all four IC families across
  $\heps \in \{0.02, 0.05, 0.10\}$, direct-isolated.
  Columns show $r_{\rm CG8}$ at each softening and the maximum
  $|r|$ across fine observables.
  The bimodal verdict is \textsc{coarse} in every cell; verdicts
  for other families vary with softening.}
\label{tab:n_scaling}
\input{outputs/tables/n_scaling.tex}
\end{table}

Physically, in a two-cluster merger the merger timescale
$t_{\rm merge} \sim d/v_{\rm rel}$ is set by the inter-cluster separation
$d$ and relative velocity, both encoded in the initial large-scale density
contrast.
The coarse grid at scale $g = 8$ ($L/8 = 0.25$, comparable to $d$)
captures exactly this contrast.
Sub-cluster internal structure is dynamically decoupled from the merger
at early times, which is why none of the tested positional fine observables
is predictive for this family.

Figure~\ref{fig:bimodal_mechanism} makes this visual.
The left panel shows the $x$--$y$ particle projection with a coarse
8$\times$8 grid overlaid.
The reported $\sigrho(8)$ is computed from the full 3D coarse observer.
The right panel shows the scatter of $\sigrho(8)$ against $\dCearly$ at
two particle counts ($N = 256$ and $N = 1024$), confirming that the
predictive relationship is stable with respect to $N$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig11_bimodal_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bimodal mechanism: the inter-cluster density contrast is the
  predictive object.
  \textit{Left}: $x$--$y$ projection of the bimodal IC with projected
  coarse-grid cells overlaid; cell shade $\propto$ projected particle count
  (illustrative; $\sigrho(8)$ is computed from the full 3D field).
  \textit{Right}: $\sigrho(8)$ vs $\dCearly$ at $N = 256$ (circles) and
  $N = 1024$ (squares), $\heps = 0.05$.
  The negative association persists across particle count.}
\label{fig:bimodal_mechanism}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Verdict map}
\label{sec:results:verdict_map}

Figure~\ref{fig:verdict_map} shows the verdict for all IC families,
softening values, and both force models at $N = 1024$.
The bimodal family is uniformly \textsc{coarse} across all cells of
both panels.
Concentrated profiles show a fine-leaning point-estimate pattern at
$\heps = 0.02$ that weakens toward tie or \textsc{coarse} by $\heps = 0.10$.
The two model classes agree on the bimodal verdict at all $\heps$.

\textit{Note on inferential strength.} The verdict map is a
point-estimate classification: cells are labelled \textsc{coarse} if
$|r_{\rm best\,coarse}| - |r_{\rm best\,fine}|$ exceeds $+0.05$,
\textsc{fine} if it falls below $-0.05$, and tie if it lies in between.
Inferential strength is assessed separately by bootstrap CIs:
the bimodal coarse result is robustly established (CIs exclude zero),
while the suggestive fine-leaning pattern for concentrated profiles at $\heps = 0.02$
has CIs that include zero and is therefore not confirmed at standard significance.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig03_verdict_map.pdf}
\caption{Verdict map at $N = 1024$, primary target $\dCearly$.
  Each cell shows $r_C$ (best coarse) and $r_f$ (best fine).
  Blue: \textsc{coarse}.  Green: \textsc{fine}.  Grey: tie.
  \textit{Left}: direct-isolated.  \textit{Right}: PM-periodic.
  Bimodal is \textsc{coarse} in all cells of both panels.}
\label{fig:verdict_map}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Time evolution}
\label{sec:results:snapshots}

Figure~\ref{fig:snapshots} shows projected-density snapshots for three
representative cases: the bimodal coarse-win anchor, the Hernquist
suggestive fine-leaning case at $\heps = 0.02$, and the Hernquist boundary
case at $\heps = 0.10$.

In the bimodal case the two sub-clusters merge along the $x$-axis;
the bridge forms by the early horizon and a single object is present at
final time.
In the Hernquist case at $\heps = 0.02$ the cusp retains its gradient
at early times, and the velocity-dispersion field is spatially structured.
At $\heps = 0.10$ softening washes out the cusp dynamics and the
kinematic observable loses its early-time structure.

\subsection{Suggestive fine-leaning at small softening}
\label{sec:results:cond_fine}

For concentrated profiles at small softening, the local velocity dispersion
shows the strongest fine signal in the battery.
Table~\ref{tab:cond_fine} shows VelDisp and kNN-all correlations at
$\heps = 0.02$ for Hernquist, Plummer, and bimodal at $N = 1024$.
For Hernquist: $r_{\rm VD} = \HernquistVelDispR{}$
(95\% CI $[\HernquistVelDispCILo{}, \HernquistVelDispCIHi{}]$).
For Plummer: $r_{\rm VD} = \PlummerVelDispR{}$
(95\% CI $[\PlummerVelDispCILo{}, \PlummerVelDispCIHi{}]$).
Both 95\% CIs include zero; the pattern is suggestive but not robustly
established at standard significance with the current replicate count.
The kNN-all positional observable does not outperform the coarse predictor
for any family ($r_{\rm kNN} = \HernquistKNNR{}$ for Hernquist at this cell).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{VelDisp and kNN-all correlations across all three softening
  values for Hernquist and Plummer at $N = 1024$, direct-isolated.
  VelDisp shows the strongest fine signal for concentrated profiles
  at small softening, but all 95\% CIs that include zero are noted.
  kNN-all does not outperform the coarse predictor for any family.}
\label{tab:cond_fine}
\input{outputs/tables/cond_fine.tex}
\end{table}

Figure~\ref{fig:cond_fine} shows how VelDisp, kNN-all, and CoarseG8
change with $\heps$ across the three families.
For Hernquist and Plummer the VelDisp signal decays with increasing $\heps$,
reaching $r_{\rm VD} = \HernquistVelDispEpsTen{}$ for Hernquist at
$\heps = 0.10$.
The kNN-all positional observable does not outperform the coarse predictor
for any family at any tested $\heps$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig05_cond_fine.pdf}
\caption{Observable class vs softening: $N = 1024$, direct-isolated.
  Solid: VelDisp (kinematic fine).
  Dashed: kNN-all (positional fine).
  Dotted: CoarseG8 (coarse).
  Shaded: 95\% bootstrap CI.
  The VelDisp signal is present at $\heps = 0.02$ for concentrated profiles
  and weakens with increasing $\heps$.
  kNN-all does not outperform the coarse predictor in any cell tested.}
\label{fig:cond_fine}
\end{figure}

A plausible mechanism is local virial support.
In a Hernquist or Plummer profile, particles near the cusp have high
velocity dispersion relative to their local escape velocity; these
kinematically hot regions resist collapse.
The VelDisp observable at $t = 0$ appears to track this pressure distribution.
Tested positional fine observables carry no velocity information and
cannot detect it.
The suggestive fine-leaning VelDisp signal is observable-class-specific: it requires phase-space access.

Figure~\ref{fig:veldisp_mechanism} illustrates why softening destroys this
signal.
At $\heps = 0.02$ (top row) the projected density shows the cusp
structure, the local velocity-dispersion map reveals a spatially
concentrated hot core, and the radial profile $\sigma_v(r)$ is steeply
peaked at small $r$.
At $\heps = 0.10$ (bottom row) the density map is smoothed,
the velocity-dispersion map loses its central concentration, and the
radial profile flattens.
When $\heps/a \approx 0.5$, the cusp dynamics are suppressed and
the kinematic fine signal disappears.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig12_veldisp_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{VelDisp mechanism: Hernquist profile, $N = \ShowcaseN{}$.
  \textit{Rows}: $\heps = 0.02$ (top); $\heps = 0.10$ (bottom).
  \textit{Columns}: projected density (log scale); local
  velocity-dispersion map; median $\sigma_v^{\rm loc}(r)$ vs radius.
  At small softening the kinematic structure is concentrated toward the
  cusp; at large softening it is washed out.}
\label{fig:veldisp_mechanism}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The softening transition}
\label{sec:results:eps_transition}

Figure~\ref{fig:eps_transition} shows for all four families how the
coarse advantage $|r_{\rm coarse}| - |r_{\rm best\,fine}|$ changes
with $\heps$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig06_eps_transition.pdf}
\caption{Coarse advantage vs softening: $N = 1024$, direct-isolated.
  Each curve shows $|r_{\rm coarse}| - |r_{\rm best\,fine}|$ as a function
  of $\heps$ for one IC family.
  Bimodal maintains a large positive advantage at all $\heps$.
  Concentrated profiles show a suggestive fine-leaning signal at
  $\heps = 0.02$ that weakens to tie or coarse-favoured by $\heps = 0.10$.}
\label{fig:eps_transition}
\end{figure}

Bimodal maintains a large positive coarse advantage at all tested $\heps$
because the dynamically decisive scale ($\sim 0.5\,L$) is far above
the softening length in every cell.
For Hernquist and Plummer the coarse advantage shifts from negative,
corresponding to a suggestive fine-leaning point-estimate pattern,
at $\heps = 0.02$ toward zero or positive (coarse-favoured or tied)
at $\heps = 0.10$.
The transition is not sharply resolved on the three-point $\heps$ grid.
The relevant dimensionless ratio appears to be $\heps/a$: the cusp is
partially resolved at $\heps/a = 0.10$ ($\heps = 0.02$) and smoothed out
at $\heps/a = 0.50$ ($\heps = 0.10$).

Figure~\ref{fig:eps_boundary} plots the coarse advantage directly against
$\heps/a$ for all four IC families.
The bimodal curve stays high and positive throughout; the cold-clumpy
curve is mixed.
For Hernquist and Plummer the transition from a suggestive fine-leaning
signal (negative coarse advantage) to zero or positive coarse advantage
occurs between $\heps/a \approx 0.10$ and
$\heps/a \approx 0.50$; the shaded region marks this unresolved transition
zone.
A finer sweep in $\heps/a$ would be needed to locate the boundary precisely.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig13_eps_boundary.pdf}
\caption{Verdict boundary in $\heps/a$: coarse advantage
  $|r_{\rm coarse}| - |r_{\rm best\,fine}|$ vs the softening-to-scale-radius
  ratio, $N = 1024$, direct-isolated.
  Each point is annotated with the verdict (C = \textsc{coarse},
  F = \textsc{fine}, T = tie).
  Bimodal stays above zero at all tested $\heps/a$.
  Hernquist and Plummer show a suggestive fine-leaning signal at
  $\heps/a \approx 0.10$ that shifts toward zero or positive between
  $\heps/a \approx 0.10$ and $0.50$ (shaded zone).}
\label{fig:eps_boundary}
\end{figure}

\subsection{N-scaling}
\label{sec:results:n_scaling}

Figure~\ref{fig:n_scaling} shows $r_{\rm CG8}$ and the best fine predictor
vs $N$ for all four families, at each $\heps$ value.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig07_n_scaling.pdf}
\caption{N-scaling at three softening values, direct-isolated.
  Each panel: one IC family.
  Coloured lines: $r_{\rm CG8}$ (solid/dashed/dotted for
  $\heps = 0.02/0.05/0.10$).
  Grey: best fine predictor.
  Bimodal is stable near $-0.98$ at all $N$ and $\heps$.}
\label{fig:n_scaling}
\end{figure}

For bimodal, the coarse predictor is stable across $N \in [\NParticleMin{},
\NParticleMax{}]$ at all $\heps$; the verdict does not change with particle
count.
For Hernquist and Plummer, VelDisp improves modestly with $N$ (kNN
neighbourhoods become better resolved), but the same suggestive fine-leaning
VelDisp pattern appears across all tested $N$ at small $\heps$.
There is no evidence of a verdict reversal as $N$ increases.

\subsection{Force-model comparison}
\label{sec:results:model_compare}

Figure~\ref{fig:model_comparison} shows $r_{\rm CG8}$ vs $\heps$ for
both model classes at $N = 1024$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig08_model_comparison.pdf}
\caption{Force-model comparison: $r_{\rm CG8}$ vs $\heps$, $N = 1024$.
  Blue: direct-isolated.  Brown: PM-periodic.
  Shaded: 95\% CI.
  Both models agree on the bimodal verdict.
  Concentrated profiles show quantitative differences but the same
  qualitative pattern.}
\label{fig:model_comparison}
\end{figure}

The two model classes agree on the bimodal verdict for all tested $\heps$.
For concentrated profiles, quantitative differences exist because the PM
force resolution ($\sim L/32$) smooths sub-resolution structure differently
from the softened direct-sum potential.
Note that in the PM-periodic implementation used here, the force resolution
is set primarily by the mesh spacing ($\sim L/32$), so changing the reported
$\heps$ parameter has little effect on the dynamics; PM rows are therefore
nearly $\heps$-invariant.
The direct-isolated results show the clearest $\heps$-dependent transition
for Hernquist and Plummer; the PM-periodic implementation preserves the
qualitative family-level verdict structure but is nearly $\heps$-invariant
because its force resolution is set by the mesh rather than $\heps$.

\subsection{Observable-class dependence}
\label{sec:results:obs_class}

The main verdict table (Table~\ref{tab:verdict_summary}) summarises
verdicts across both force-model classes, all initial-condition families,
and all softening values at $N = 1024$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Verdict summary at $N = 1024$, both force-model classes,
  all initial-condition families, and $\heps \in \{0.02, 0.05, 0.10\}$.
  Gap column shows $|r_{\rm best\,fine}| - |r_{\rm best\,coarse}|$.}
\label{tab:verdict_summary}
\input{outputs/tables/verdict_summary.tex}
\end{table}

Three patterns hold across the battery.
First, none of the three tested positional fine observables (kNN-all, Pk,
ClosePairs) outperforms the coarse predictor for any IC family at any
tested $\heps$ or $N$; the coarse advantage is robust even when individual
positional fine correlations are non-negligible.
Second, the FoF group count is not a reliable predictor in any tested cell.
Third, VelDisp shows the strongest fine signal, but only for concentrated
profiles at small $\heps$, and with 95\% CIs that include zero at the
current replicate count.

\subsection{Summary matrix}
\label{sec:results:summary}

Figure~\ref{fig:summary_matrix} shows $r$ for all observable class
$\times$ $\heps$ combinations as a colour matrix.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{outputs/figures/fig10_summary_matrix.pdf}
\caption{Summary matrix: Pearson $r$ with $\dCearly$ by IC family (rows),
  observable class (groups), and $\heps$ (within-group columns),
  at $N = 1024$, direct-isolated.
  The coarse group (leftmost) shows strong negative $r$ for bimodal at all
  $\heps$.

  in any cell.}
\label{fig:summary_matrix}

The matrix makes the observable-class structure visible.
The coarse column shows the largest and most consistent signal for bimodal
across all $\heps$.
The VelDisp column shows a suggestive fine-leaning signal for Hernquist and Plummer at
$\heps = 0.02$ that fades at $\heps = 0.10$.
The positional fine columns show non-negligible $r$ values in some cells,
but in no tested cell does a positional fine observable outperform the
coarse predictor.


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Physical interpretation: bimodal case}

In a two-cluster merger the dominant dynamical variable is the inter-cluster
density contrast.
The merger timescale $t_{\rm merge} \sim d/v_{\rm rel}$ is set by
quantities that are encoded in the large-scale density field, not in
sub-cluster internal packing.
The coarse density variance $\sigrho(8)$ at grid scale $L/8 \approx 0.25$
captures this contrast directly.
Realisations with higher initial $\sigrho(8)$ have larger contrast and
shorter merger timescales, producing more clustering growth by the early
horizon.
Sub-cluster kNN density, Fourier power at small scales, and close-pair
fraction do not outperform the coarse predictor in this family in this battery.

\subsection{Physical interpretation: concentrated profiles}

In an approximately virialised system the local velocity dispersion encodes
kinematic pressure.
Regions with higher initial $\sigma_v^{\rm loc}$ have more virial support
and resist collapse, producing a negative correlation between VelDisp at
$t = 0$ and future clustering growth.
Tested positional fine observables cannot detect this because a virial-equilibrium
density profile is approximately smooth above the softening scale; kNN
density and pair statistics do not resolve structure correlated with the
velocity-dispersion distribution.
The suggestive fine-leaning VelDisp signal is observable-class-specific: it requires
access to the velocity field, and the 95\% CIs do not exclude zero at the
current sample size, so it is better described as suggestive than established.

Increasing $\heps$ suppresses this mechanism by smoothing the potential
over scales comparable to the cusp scale radius.
The relevant ratio appears to be $\heps/a$; the boundary between fine-leaning
and coarse-favoured in this battery lies between $\heps/a \approx 0.10$ and
$\heps/a \approx 0.50$, but is not sharply localised on the three-point
$\heps$ grid used here.

\subsection{What is and is not earned}
\label{sec:discussion:scope}

\textbf{Earned within this battery:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Robust coarse dominance for bimodal (two-cluster) ICs, stable
    across all tested $N$, $\heps$, and force-model classes.
  \item No tested positional fine observable outperforms the coarse predictor
    in any tested cell (kNN-all, Pk, ClosePairs across all families, $N$,
    and $\heps$).
  \item The boundary appears to be governed in part by $\heps/a$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Suggestive but not yet earned:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item A VelDisp fine-leaning signal for Hernquist and Plummer at
    $\heps = 0.02$.
    Both 95\% CIs include zero; the pattern is directionally consistent
    but not robustly established at standard significance.
    A larger replicate count or an explicit power analysis is needed
    before this can be treated as a confirmed result.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Not earned:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Universal coarse dominance in 3D self-gravitating systems.
  \item Universal fine superiority of any kind.
  \item A causal-handle result (this study measures correlation,
    not causation).
  \item Cosmological generalisation (no expansion, cooling, or feedback).
  \item A sharp boundary location in $\heps/a$ (transition unresolved
    on 3-point grid).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Scope and limitations}

The prediction target is a single scalar ($\dCearly$).
Fine observables might carry more information for spatially resolved targets
or longer prediction horizons; this is not tested here.

The $\heps$ grid (0.02, 0.05, 0.10) does not sharply locate the
transition for concentrated profiles.
A finer sweep would narrow the boundary in $\heps/a$.


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We have presented a battery of \TotalRuns{} simulations covering
$N \in [\NParticleMin{}, \NParticleMax{}]$, softening
$\heps \in [\EpsMin{}, \EpsMax{}]$, \NICs{} initial condition families,
and \NModels{} force-model classes, with \NReplicates{} replicates per cell.

Bimodal initial conditions define a robust coarse-dominance regime.
The coarse density variance predicts future clustering at
$r = \BimodalCoarseR{}$ (CI $[\BimodalCoarseCILo{}, \BimodalCoarseCIHi{}]$)
at $N = 1024$, $\heps = 0.05$, with the verdict unchanged from
$N = \NParticleMin{}$ to $\NParticleMax{}$, from $\heps = \EpsMin{}$ to
$\heps = \EpsMax{}$, and across both force-model classes.
None of the three tested positional fine observables outperforms the
coarse predictor for this family in any tested cell.

Concentrated profiles (Hernquist, Plummer) show a suggestive fine-leaning VelDisp
signal at $\heps = \EpsMin{}$; both 95\% confidence intervals include
zero; this pattern warrants follow-up with increased replicates or an
explicit power analysis.
The signal weakens substantially by $\heps = \EpsMax{}$; the boundary
appears to be governed in part by the softening-to-scale-radius ratio.
None of the tested positional fine observables outperforms the coarse
predictor for concentrated profiles at any tested $\heps$.

The central empirical result is the verdict asymmetry between observable
classes: no tested positional fine observable outperforms the coarse
predictor in any cell, while the kinematic fine observable (VelDisp) shows
a suggestive fine-leaning pattern for concentrated profiles at small
softening.
The tested fine kinematic observable, VelDisp, can show a suggestive
advantage, but only when the observable class, the IC family (concentrated
cusp), and the softening regime (small $\heps/a$) are all simultaneously
satisfied---and even then the result requires replication to establish
robustly.
